name: New Thought
scope: New Thought as its defining sources describe it: the mind-healing, metaphysical and religious movement that began in the United States in the 19th century with Phineas P. Quimby and the systematizing of his ideas by Warren F. Evans and Julius Dresser (s1, s2, s3). It holds the immanence of God, the divine nature of humanity, the spiritual character of the universe and that sin, disorder and disease are matters of incorrect thinking, so that people can live in oneness with God in love, truth, peace, health and plenty (s1). It takes in the groups that grew from Quimby's followers (Divine Science, Unity, Religious Science, Home of Truth) and the National, later International, New Thought Alliance, whose 1917 Declaration of Principles states its common affirmations (s1, s2, s3), and its writers such as Atkinson, Fillmore, Troward, Trine, Towne and Wilcox (s1, s3). It is a spiritual movement: the audit records only political ideas of what society should be that these sources or the key figures' texts state, and leaves out Christian Science (Mary Baker Eddy's separate church, s2), Theosophy, and later self-help or prosperity-gospel offshoots except as the sources tie them to the movement.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Atkinson, The Law of the New Thought, ch. I (p. 9ff.): New Thought 'contains within it only that which may be found in all the great religions of the world'; ch. XI (p. 62ff.): followers of different creeds name Jehovah, Buddha, Brahma or Allah, 'But they all meant the same thing — GOD'.

god-not-male.rationale: Atkinson, The Law of the New Thought, ch. XI (p. 66): he uses 'him' only by convention, 'not because I consider him as being masculine'; 'GOD has no sex', combining 'both the Father-Mother elements'.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Towne, How to Use New Thought in Home Life, ch. 'What I Think About Marriage and Divorce' (pp. 174-178): the right of every individual 'to make or break marriage according to the dictates of his own conscience'; divorce is 'matrimonial bankruptcy', and 'To make divorce difficult is to maintain a matrimonial debtor's prison'. She gives personal views she expects most New Thought people to share.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Towne, How to Use New Thought in Home Life, ch. 'What I Think About Marriage and Divorce' (pp. 176-178): the right of 'every individual' to make or break marriage by conscience, and society should 'be forgiving even to seventy times seven divorces'; no husband's consent is required.

women-suffrage.rationale: Towne, How to Use New Thought in Home Life, ch. 'What I Think About Marriage and Divorce' (p. 177): 'give women the ballot and equality of earning power with men'.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Towne, How to Use New Thought in Home Life, p. 175-176: the New Thought ideal of all as 'equal heirs to all riches' is 'destined to express itself in equal distribution of wealth, education, and opportunity to every man, woman, and child'. Her personal view, stated as New Thought's.

public-ownership.rationale: Trine, In the Fire of the Heart, ch. VI 'Public Utilities for the Public Good' (e.g. pp. 132, 165): endorses government ownership and management of railways and other utilities. It covers public utilities, not all major industries.

unions-good.rationale: Trine, In the Fire of the Heart, ch. VII 'Labour and its Uniting Power' (pp. 193-196): approves of labour unions, quoting that workers without them would be in a condition 'to shock the mind', while allowing that unions 'have committed errors'.

direct-votes.rationale: Trine, In the Fire of the Heart, ch. VIII (pp. 240-242): 'It is through the principle of Direct Legislation, by means of the Initiative and Referendum, that we can get the machinery of government back into our own hands.'

recall-officials.rationale: Trine, In the Fire of the Heart, ch. VIII (p. 270): advocates 'the Recall': an official too subservient to corporations or the people's will 'can, upon petition of a stipulated number of voters ... be recalled and retired'.

corporate-influence.rationale: Trine, In the Fire of the Heart, ch. V 'A Great People's Movement' (p. 105) and ch. VIII (p. 270): complains that 'capital controls legislation' and officials become 'subservient to the interests of public-service corporations, trusts, combines'.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Trine, In the Fire of the Heart, ch. V (pp. 108-109): a privileged few take enormous wealth through franchises while 'concentrated wealth and power' stifle 'the idea of greater equality and justice'.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Wilcox, New Thought Common Sense, 'Building Kindness Cells' (pp. 243-245): urges parents to attend 'to the rights of animals' and to avoid 'the suffering it gives other human beings or animals'; 'treat each human being and animal as you would wish to be treated'.

summary: New Thought is a loose American spiritual movement from the 1860s on (Quimby, Evans, the Dressers, later Atkinson, Fillmore, Troward, Trine, Towne and Wilcox) that holds mind and thought shape health and circumstance and that God is an immanent spirit present in everyone. It has no creed and claims to share the core of all religions. Its core texts are spiritual and almost silent on politics, so only a few answers come from key figures' own writing on marriage, reform and labour.

notes: Themes searched in the key figures' texts: government, economics and labour, democracy, marriage and divorce, women, religion and God, war and peace, animals, punishment, health policy. Core New Thought sources are silent on most; positions come from Towne (marriage), Atkinson (religion, God), Wilcox (animals) and Trine (reform politics). Trine's and Towne's views are individual authors', not a movement platform; Towne says as much, and confidence is medium throughout.
